A dramatic scene took place regularly on the first of every month in the small cottage of the old General and Madame B----.
The monthly scene began with Madame B---- waking the General, standing at his bedside with a cup of black coffee.
On the first of the month the General had affairs to transact.
On mornings when affairs were to be transacted, the household had little leisure.
Honorine was the entire household.
On those mornings the General did not wear his old dressing-gown, slippers, very old trousers and old-fashioned neck scarf.
On those mornings the General washed in warm water with a dash of cologne in it.
Honorine trimmed the General's beard and mustache.
The General dressed in a black broadcloth suit and a brown satin stock.
The General had an easy, casual elegance that no one could possess or put on as well as he could.
It is uncertain whether the fine manners of gentlemen of the General's day were natural or put on.
Gentlemen of the General's generation spent their youth in Paris acquiring good manners and an education.
The first of the month was also a kind of holiday for Madame la Générale.
Old wives enjoy seeing their husbands dressed up in the manners and graces that won them when they were young.
A woman likes to celebrate her conquest of her husband until the end of her life.
For a woman, the worst misfortune is to see her youthful husband become old, ugly and commonplace.
Under their gray hair and wrinkles, old women still feel flutterings, thrills and strong emotions.
The passions of a woman's heart go out only at death.
Honorine's hands went cold, as they had at sixteen, when she brought the scissors to the General's white mustache and beard.
The General's lips were still well formed and rosy.
When Honorine's fingertips brushed the General's lips, she felt the touch on her own lips.
Buying the cologne was Honorine's secret delight and her greatest effort at saving money.
When Honorine added cologne to the water, she always felt a brief faintness.
The faintness was the same one she had felt as a bride leaving the church with the General.
Honorine first noticed the faint smell of the cologne bath as a bride.
Honorine looked forward from month to month to the thoughts she had during this moment.
The General had been a very handsome man.
The General belonged to a period that demanded physical beauty from Nature.
Nature always gives each period what it demands.
If a period produces small men, or even gnomes and dwarfs, it is because the period demands them from Nature.
Getting dressed was a ceremony for the General.
After dressing, the General had chocolate and pain de Paris for breakfast.
Honorine could not imagine the General eating anything but pain de Paris for breakfast.
After breakfast the General sat in his large armchair at his writing desk to transact his affairs.
Pompey brought the General his mail.
The General called Pompey an idiot, a dolt, a sluggard and a snail for not yet having arrived with the mail.
The General insisted that Pompey should already have arrived, since it was nine o'clock and he was ready.
Honorine told him it was not yet nine o'clock.
Honorine was washing the General's cup, saucer and spoon in the next room.
Honorine always agreed with her husband promptly and cheerfully.
The General claimed that Pompey was getting worse every day, was worthless and trifling, and should be discharged.
Honorine urged her husband to have patience.
Honorine's one fault was that she never learned from experience.
The General held that patience is an invention of dullards and sluggards.
The General held that in a well-regulated world there would be no need for patience.
The General said patience should be punished as a crime, or at least as a breach of the peace, and investigated by police like smallpox.
The General claimed he never heard the word "patience" in Paris.
The General claimed that in Paris a messenger who asked for patience would be beaten with a walking stick and told that legs, not professors of patience, were being hired.
The General and Honorine did not pay Pompey.
Pompey fetched the mail out of kindness, to oblige them.
The General scorned the idea that a Black man could oblige him or be kind to him.
The General saw talk of favor, obliging, education, and "monsieur" and "madame" as typical of the new regime.
The General considered it childish to call the present order a country or a government.
The General suspected that the mail had been tampered with.
The General did not trust the honesty of postal officials and called it a farce.
The General concluded that Pompey had failed to find the letter in the box.
The General had yet another theory for why his mail was late, which he always brought up abruptly after he had finished attacking the post office.
